title: Attribute test failures via baseline diff, not absolute counts
body: The full pytest suite has a large population (~140) of pre-existing failures in sandboxes lacking real backends (LanceDB/PostgreSQL) and where the embedding model can't load (SentenceTransformer/torch on Apple MPS: 'Cannot copy out of meta tensor' — set INQUIRY_EMBEDDING_DEVICE=cpu to dodge it). The suite also randomizes order (pytest-randomly), so failure positions and even which flaky tests fail shift run to run; absolute pass/fail counts are not comparable across runs. To decide whether a change introduced a regression, diff the FAILING-TEST SETS between your branch and origin/main with identical flags (e.g. via --junitxml + set difference), not the totals. Use -p no:randomly for a deterministic run.

title: uv.lock bumps churn markers when your uv is newer than origin/main's
body: Running `uv lock --upgrade-package X` with a uv newer than the one that generated the committed uv.lock regenerates the whole file, normalizing/simplifying redundant environment markers across packages unrelated to X (seen with cloud-sql-python-connector, scipy/numpy, hypothesis, nvidia-* CUDA, secretstorage). Why 'redundant': older uv emitted conservatively narrowed per-dependency markers (e.g. `python_full_version < '3.13'` on a sub-dep whose parent is already gated `< '3.13'`, or `>= '3.10.2'` floors implied by requires-python >=3.10); newer uv recomputes markers against the package's actual support range and drops the ones already implied by an enclosing marker or by requires-python. The installed set is identical (no package add/remove) and `uv lock --locked` still passes, so it's semantically benign — but it bloats a focused dependency PR's diff. For a minimal diff, regenerate with the same uv version that produced origin/main's lock; otherwise just note the benign churn in the PR/commit body so reviewers aren't surprised.

title: Connector registration is an import-time decorator side effect — fragile two ways
body: Connectors register via `@register_connector("name")` in their module; the registry's `_register_builtin_connectors()` only makes them reachable by *importing* the module (firing the decorator). Two consequences bit us in issue #82. (1) A connector whose module nothing imports is silently unregistered: `GCSConnector` carried `@register_connector("gcs")` but `_register_builtin_connectors()` never imported it (only s3/filesystem), so `get_connector("gcs")` raised KeyError despite the class existing — fix was to add the guarded `from ...gcs import GCSConnector` import. The lib check (gcsfs/s3fs) lives in `__init__`, not at module import, so registration works even without the cloud lib installed — only construction needs it. (2) Because Python caches modules, the decorator fires only on FIRST import; after `ConnectorRegistry.reset_instance()` the decorators do NOT re-fire, so `_register_builtin_connectors()` cannot restore s3/gcs (only the explicitly-registered filesystem/file). test_registry.py reset the singleton in autouse fixtures without restoring, leaking an empty registry to later test files — invisible while s3fs/gcsfs are absent (those registration tests skip) but a hard failure once the extras are installed. Robust test pattern: snapshot the registered factories at import time and re-register them on teardown; assert import-time registration in a fresh subprocess interpreter, not in-process (sibling tests that import the connector module pollute the in-process registry and make the assertion pass for the wrong reason).

title: fsspec connector URI scheme and fsspec protocol are independent
body: In an FsspecConnector subclass the `protocol=` passed to the base (what `fsspec.filesystem()` receives) and the URI scheme emitted by `_build_uri`/parsed by `_uri_to_path` are separate concerns. GCSConnector passes `protocol="gcs"` (gcsfs accepts it) but its `SourceItem.uri` scheme is cosmetic and feeds `SourceItem.protocol`. We aligned the URI scheme from `gs://` to `gcs://` to match the registered connector name, `item.protocol`, and the docs — without touching the fsspec protocol. Don't 'fix' one to match the other. Also note gcsfs's real `md5Hash` is base64-encoded (e.g. 'CY9rzUYh03PK3k6DJie09g=='), not hex; `base._extract_hash` passes it through verbatim (its `strip('"')` is S3-ETag cleanup), so mocks using plain ASCII hashes hide the real shape — pin the base64 pass-through explicitly.

title: Call-graph extraction must probe tree-sitter node fields/types per grammar, not hardcode Python's
body: The `queries/*.scm` files correctly capture calls for every language, but `_extract_call_info` and `_find_containing_definition[_key]` used to hardcode Python's grammar — the `function` field and `identifier`/`attribute` node types, and container types `function_definition`/`class_definition`/`method_definition`. So Java (`method_invocation` with `name`/`object` fields; containers `method_declaration`/`class_declaration`) and Rust (`field_expression` method calls; `function_item`/`impl_item`) produced ZERO `calls` edges even though entities extracted fine (issue #179). Fix: probe structure — prefer the `function` field (Python `call`, C-family/Go/Rust/TS/C# `call_expression`/`invocation_expression`), else fall back to `name`/`method` + `object`/`receiver` (Java, Ruby). Node type `call` is AMBIGUOUS: Python's has a `function` field, Ruby's has `method`/`receiver` — so a naive node-type dispatch silently regresses Ruby. Three more traps: (1) only add a node type to `_DEFINITION_NODE_TYPES` if it's captured as a processable `.def`/element — `arrow_function` (`@code_function.arrow`) and Rust `mod_item` (`@code_module`) are NOT, and would silently swallow the calls attributed to them; container byte-span must line up with an emitted `@code_*.def` element or the edge is dropped. (2) The collection loop de-dups DEFINITIONS via `seen_nodes` but did not de-dup CALLS — a call site captured under multiple query patterns (e.g. `cpp.scm` ships two byte-identical `@call.method` patterns; Java captures the same invocation as both `@call` and `@call.method`) double-counts. De-dup calls by call-node byte span. (3) When the `function` field holds a member/attribute accessor, its object/name subfields vary even for the SAME accessor node-type name: Rust `field_expression` uses `value` but C++'s uses `argument` (both `field` for the name); Go method calls use `selector_expression` (`operand`/`field`). Let the object slot list multiple candidate field names and take the first that resolves, else receiver metadata silently drops to empty — the target stays correct, so a target-only test won't catch it; assert `metadata['object']`. Regression tests live in tests/parsers/test_calls_extraction_multilang.py; the Python tests in test_relationship_extraction.py are the passing baseline.

title: Narrowing requires-python needs a full sweep of version statements
body: When you change the package's supported Python range (requires-python in pyproject.toml), the declared version lives in more than pyproject + README. Grep docs for package-level prerequisites ('Python X or higher', 'X+', 'Should be X+') and update every one — a missed line (e.g. docs/mcp/deployment.md System Requirements) keeps advertising a version you no longer support. Crucially, distinguish three classes before editing: (1) package-level supported-version statements — UPDATE these; (2) dependency-specific notes (e.g. 'cloud-sql-python-connector doesn't support 3.13' in docs/backends, docs/storage) — LEAVE, they track a library's own matrix; (3) language-feature notes ('deprecated in Python 3.10+' in docs/development/async-best-practices.md) — LEAVE, they track language behavior. Also verify the co-located declarations that may not exist: pyproject classifiers, [tool.ruff] target-version (inferred from requires-python when unset), [tool.mypy] python_version (a floor, unaffected by an upper bound), and any CI matrix. See K-0002 for the companion uv.lock regeneration gotcha.

title: Read-modify-write a whole LanceDB row loses updates and duplicates rows
body: Changing a few fields of a stored row by reading the item, mutating it, then deleting and re-adding the row takes two commits and rewrites every column. Any overlapping writer of the same id (the memory layers' fire-and-forget access-stat task that retrieve() starts is one) interleaves with it: both read, both delete, both add. The table then holds two rows for one id, and a limit=1 get_by_id returns whichever was inserted first, so the caller's update is lost about half the time (the flaky test_store_retrieve_update_delete). A lock around the re-read does not help, because the stale write-back is the problem, not the read. Change fields with a single native `table.update(where, values)` (LanceDBManager.update_by_ids; memory layers' update_fields / storage.update) that names only the columns you change. To find this class of bug, wrap the adapter's get_by_id/delete/store and print asyncio.current_task().get_name() with the field values: the interleaving shows up in one run. To pin it in a test deterministically, monkeypatch the adapter's get_by_id so another writer commits right after the first read.

title: A mypy error behind a broad except is often a live runtime defect
body: Several mypy errors on main were real crashes that a surrounding `except Exception` turned into a log line or an empty result: an undefined name on the FTS stale-table retry path, a `ParsedDocument` built with a nonexistent `relationships` kwarg (oversized-document skip), `MemoryContext` missing a required `conversation_id` (REST memory store/recall always failed), and a string passed as `_poll_embedding_completion`'s `poll_interval`. Before silencing a call-arg, name-defined or arg-type error, trace the enclosing try/except: if the error would raise at runtime, fix the code and add a regression test that fails on main. The reverse also holds: when a correct annotation would change live behaviour (e.g. rejecting raw text that LanceDB currently turns into FTS), keep the behaviour, add a coded `type: ignore` with a reason, and record the gap in docs/backlog.md. And mock the real return type in tests: a REST recall test that mocked `retrieve` with dicts hid that the formatter mishandled `RetrievalResult`.

title: An unclosed EventStore or StorageFacade keeps the process alive after its work
body: EventStore, SQLiteEventStorage and StorageFacade (which opens a SQLiteEventStorage by default) each hold an aiosqlite writer connection, and every aiosqlite connection runs a non-daemon thread blocked on a queue until close(). Interpreter shutdown joins non-daemon threads, so a command or test that opens one and never closes it prints its result and then hangs forever (seen: ai memory save, ai mcp over stdio). Close in the scope that opened it: close_mcp_services for create_mcp_services, close_memory_system for create_memory_system, a finally or fixture teardown otherwise. Reading from an EventStore after close() silently reopens its writer. In pytest, tests/helpers/thread_watchdog.py names any such thread 10s into shutdown and fails the run; idle ThreadPoolExecutor workers are not leaks (concurrent.futures joins them at exit). To find where a leaked thread was started, patch threading.Thread.start to record traceback.extract_stack() and dump survivors from a tryfirst pytest_sessionfinish.

title: Config.load validates a project config as written, with no merge over default.yaml
body: Config.load reads agentic-inquiry.yaml (or --config, or INQUIRY_CONFIG) and validates it against config/config.schema.json before anything fills in defaults; only load_with_overlay deep-merges over config/default.yaml. So every config we ship or tell users to copy must be complete on its own: storage, cache, search, embeddings and parsers are required objects, with nested required keys (cache.document_cache.max_size, search.default_limit/max_limit, embeddings.default_provider). A section header with every child commented out parses as None; before the schema even runs, _validate_config calls .get on it and crashes with AttributeError. In examples, comment out an optional section's header together with its children, and give required sections real values. tests/unit/test_config.py::TestShippedConfigs loads each shipped full config the way a user would; add new ones there. validate_storage_paths also rejects a storage root whose parent directory is missing, so a root nested under the gitignored ./.agentic-inquiry/ fails on a fresh clone; test-lancedb.yaml uses ./.agentic-inquiry_test for that reason.

title: Don't blanket-banner live pages when removing a subsystem
body: The local-only cut put one 'Historical reference' banner on 19 pages, including live ones (docs/mcp/security.md, connector-guide.md, CONVENTIONS.md) whose only fault was a stray PostgreSQL line, while pages that were entirely about the removed backend kept 'Status: Current' and stayed listed in docs/README.md. Readers then can't tell live docs from dead ones, and the supported-path text survives under the banner. When removing a subsystem: delete pages that exist only to document it (fix inbound links, the docs index and skills that point at them), edit the removed paths out of live pages, and banner only pages deliberately kept as design input, naming them from the page that owns that decision (docs/storage-backends.md for storage). Verify config snippets you keep by loading them, since removed-era snippets often use keys the current schema rejects (uri vs database_path).

title: default.yaml is a merge base: users can add or override keys, never remove them
body: Config.load() deep-merges the one selected user config file (explicit path, INQUIRY_CONFIG, ./agentic-inquiry.yaml, ~/.agentic-inquiry/config.yaml) over config/default.yaml, and env overlays stack on top. Mappings merge key by key; lists and scalars replace. So every key you put in a default.yaml mapping reaches every user, and a user file cannot delete it. Keep free-form mappings that are splatted as kwargs empty in default.yaml (search.hybrid_search.reranker_params once shipped {k: 60}, which reached cross_encoder/colbert/cohere as an unexpected kwarg and silently fell back to RRF) and put the default in code instead. Keep default.yaml lists (connectors.filesystem.binary_extensions, ignore_patterns) supersets of the dataclass defaults; tests/unit/test_config.py pins that.

title: pytest terminal summary can vanish: read results from --junitxml
body: tests/conftest.py pytest_sessionfinish ends the process with os._exit, so a run can print only progress dots and no FAILED lines or totals, even for a single test file. Pass --junitxml=<path> and read failures from the XML. The XML is not written if the run is killed (for example by a shell timeout), so use pytest-timeout (--timeout=120) rather than an outer timeout to bound hanging tests.

title: Registry defaults built at import leak Config.load and mkdir into every process
body: A package __init__ that constructs its default registry entry at import (agentic_inquiry.watching did, via FileWatcher(file_tracker=FileTracker())) runs Config.load() and FileTracker's mkdir in every process that imports it, so pytest collection alone created ./.agentic-inquiry in cwd. Build the default in an _ensure_default_registered() called only by the lookups that need it (get_watcher('default'), get_watcher() with no default set, available_watchers()). Register it without set_default so a caller's default keeps precedence, and hold a threading.Lock around check-and-register because the import lock no longer serializes it. Test in a fresh interpreter through test_import_hygiene._run (scratch cwd and HOME); swap the module's FileWatcher global for a counting stub, since a real build costs about 3.5s. Precedence tests must call the building path while a caller default is set, or a set_default=True mutant still passes. agentic_inquiry/cache/__init__.py registers its lazy default with set_default=True and builds it on every get_cache(), named lookups included.

title: Config dataclass defaults are live whenever a user config file exists
body: Config.load() reads exactly one file (INQUIRY_CONFIG, ./agentic-inquiry.yaml, ~/.agentic-inquiry/config.yaml, then the packaged config/default.yaml) and does not merge a user file onto default.yaml. So a test of Config.load() in the repo root (no user file) only exercises default.yaml, while every user with their own config file runs the dataclass default for any key they omit. When you set or change a default, change the dataclass field, the schema `default` and default.yaml together; a mismatch is invisible to no-config tests. HybridSearchConfig.reranker_type sat at linear_combination while the other three said rrf. Pin a default with a Config.load() test that chdirs and points HOME at tmp_path, clears INQUIRY_* env vars, and writes a project agentic-inquiry.yaml that omits the key.

title: LanceDB merge_insert drops null-key rows and takes columns from the first record
body: Two silent data-loss behaviours of `table.merge_insert(key).when_matched_update_all().when_not_matched_insert_all()` on lancedb 0.25 / pylance 0.38. (1) A source row whose key is null is neither matched nor inserted, with no error. (2) The source columns come from the first record of the batch: a later record with an extra field has that field dropped, and a later record missing a field the first had writes null into it. Columns absent from every record keep their stored value (partial update), unlike delete-then-add, which nulls them. `_collapse_duplicate_merge_keys` also folds all null-key rows into one. `LanceDBManager.upsert()` therefore rejects keyless records (`is None` or `== ""`, not falsiness) and batches whose records have different field sets before calling `_upsert_rows`, and runs `_validate_record` itself so a schema error surfaces as ValueError rather than being wrapped as StorageError inside `_upsert_rows`. Any new merge_insert caller with heterogeneous or user-supplied rows needs the same checks.

title: Reproduce a LanceDB commit race by hooking LanceDBManager._locked
body: Every write to an existing table commits inside `LanceDBManager._locked(table_name)`, so it is the one seam where a competing writer can be run at an exact point. `tests/utils/commit_hook.py` wraps it: `on_exit` fires after each lock release (between the commits of a multi-commit write, e.g. delete then add), `on_enter` before each acquire (after all of the writer's reads). The hook's own writes do not re-trigger it. Seed the table before arming: table creation does not pass through `_locked`. Pair a race test with a direct single-commit check (`table.version` rises by exactly one), because a hook that fires on the first exit cannot tell one commit from two commits under one lock hold. To prove a writer does not rewrite columns from a stale read, bump another column before every lock entry on the item's table and assert the final value equals the number of bumps that hit a row (see `_AccessBumper` in tests/memory/test_memory_row_replace_atomicity.py).

title: MagicMock storage facades hid real storage bugs
body: Session, statistics and persistence tests mocked StorageFacade / LanceDBManager and asserted on mock calls, so they kept passing while the real paths broke: LanceDB providers rejected the Filter ASTs the facade documents, mcp_sessions inferred null-typed columns from a first row without a description, list_sessions silently scoped to the facade's project, and SessionManager read a created_at column document_chunks does not have. Run storage-facing tests against the real `lancedb_storage` fixture in tests/mcp/conftest.py (a StorageFacade over tmp_path); to exercise an error path, patch one method of the real manager to raise instead of mocking the whole object.

title: Supersedes K-0001 on ordering: pytest-randomly is not installed
body: K-0001 says the suite randomizes order via pytest-randomly. It is not a dependency of this repo, so `-p no:randomly` is a no-op and test order is deterministic. A test that fails intermittently here is racing, not order-dependent: repeat it in isolation (a loop of single-test runs) before looking for cross-test pollution. The baseline-diff advice in K-0001 still holds.

title: ruff format can move a `# type: ignore` off the line mypy reports
body: When a statement is too long even without its trailing pragma, ruff format splits it and leaves `# type: ignore[...]` on the closing paren. mypy reports the error on the statement's first line, so the suppression silently stops working. An AST comparison cannot see this, and `ruff check` parity does not catch it either. After any repo-wide `ruff format`, run `git grep -nE '^ *\)+,? *# type: ignore' -- '*.py'`, move each hit to the statement's first line, and diff mypy findings against main by file, code and message (line numbers shift). Two more traps: ruff runs over `.claude/` unless it is excluded (pack-managed files, excluded in pyproject), and the golden bench indexes this repo's own source, so a reformat changes its corpus. Re-run `tests/golden/bench.py --reindex` and compare recall. Keep the pre-commit ruff hooks on `uv run --frozen ruff`; a pinned ruff-pre-commit rev drifts from uv.lock and the formatters disagree.

title: httpx ASGITransport never runs the app lifespan
body: An app driven through `AsyncClient(transport=ASGITransport(app=app))` never receives the ASGI lifespan startup or shutdown events, so cleanup registered in the lifespan never runs and every store the app opened stays open. For create_app that meant two aiosqlite connections, each a non-daemon thread, left behind per test; tests/helpers/thread_watchdog.py then exits pytest with status 1 even when every test passed. Enter the lifespan explicitly around the client: `async with app.router.lifespan_context(app), AsyncClient(...) as client:`. To find which test leaked a thread, record each aiosqlite thread's first-seen test at teardown and list the ones alive at pytest_sessionfinish; per-test thread-count deltas mislead because many connections close later.
